tasks.registered_metrics_text:
a) Define the metric(s) to assess a property of an algorithm. These metrics should reflect the desired algorithm
properties described in assessment aim(s) (see above). State which metric(s) were used to compute the ranking(s) (if
any).

  • Example 1: Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC)

  • Example 2: Area under curve (AUC)

Average Precision (AP), which "summarizes a precision-recall curve as the weighted mean of precisions achieved
at each threshold, with the increase in recall from the previous threshold used as the weight" (https://scikitlearn.
org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.metrics.average_precision_score.html) . For more information see [9] or
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.metrics.average_precision_score.html.
Our evaluation code can be found here: https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/mood

b) Justify why the metric(s) was/were chosen, preferably with reference to the biomedical application.

We chose AP since it is more robust to AUROC with regard to class imbalance (despite us being able to control it
and keep it at 1/2 to 2/3 ) and has been suggested by many recent papers [2,3,4,6,9]. However, since this is the
among most used and often recommended metrics we chose AP, but after the challenge might investigate
different metrics, such as object-level detection metrics (choosing an abnormality threshold based on a hold-out
validation set similar to [23]) and present it in the paper as well as on the leaderboard (e.g. AUROC, FPR@95 ).

a) Describe the method used to compute a performance rank for all submitted algorithms based on the generated
metric results on the test cases. Typically the text will describe how results obtained per case and metric are




                                    Medical Out-of-Distribution Analysis Challenge 2024

aggregated to arrive at a final score/ranking.

We chose AP since it is more robust to AUROC with regard to class imbalance (despite us being able to control it
and keep it at 1/2 to 2/3 ) and has been suggested by many recent papers [2,3,4,6,9]. However, since this is the
among most used and often recommended metrics we chose AP, but after the challenge might investigate
different metrics and present them in the paper as well as on the leaderboard (e.g. AUROC, FPR@95 ).

b) Describe the method(s) used to manage submissions with missing results on test cases.

Since we use docker-based testing we assume that almost all participants will process all cases. However, should
one case be not considered, we will assign it the lowest given anomaly score (= 0).

c) Justify why the described ranking scheme(s) was/were used.

For each sample, the users should report an anomaly score, indicating the certainty of detecting the anomaly in
the given image. We expect the scores to be in the interval [0-1], where 0 is the lowest score indicating no
abnormality and 1 is the highest score indicating the most abnormal input (Scores above and below the interval
will be clamped to [0-1]). We will use the reported scores together with the ground truth labels to calculate the AP
over the whole dataset. The ranking for one dataset will then be given by the AP over the whole dataset. We
combine the two datasets by choosing a consolidation ranking schema.

tasks.registered_metrics_text:
a) Define the metric(s) to assess a property of an algorithm. These metrics should reflect the desired algorithm
properties described in assessment aim(s) (see above). State which metric(s) were used to compute the ranking(s) (if
any).

  • Example 1: Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC)

  • Example 2: Area under curve (AUC)

As it was successful for last year's edition and corresponded more closely to a human-aligned metric, in contrast
to AP, we here opt for a more object-centric metric.
Here a GT object is either given by a rendered object or a (connected) segmented (natural) anomaly.
A prediction object is obtained in the following way: The participants can decide if they want to submit a binary
prediction (0 or 1) or a continuous score (0-1). In the case of a continuous score, we use a toy-dataset (similar to
the toy-dataset presented to the participants) to determine the best binarization threshold with respect to the
presented metric on this toy-dataset. We then use the binarization threshold to binarize the continuous score. On
the binarized score, we apply connected component analysis to find individual objects and discard all objects that
are smaller than half the size of the smallest anomaly in our test set and all objects with are more than two times
bigger than the biggest object in our test set (to sort out low-frequency noise). This procedure then outputs the
prediction objects.
We then match the GT objects and the prediction objects in the following way to obtain TP, FP, FN:
If the center of mass of the prediction object falls in the convex hull of the GT object and the size difference is only
at max a factor of two (= 0.5 * GT-object size < prediction-object size < 2*GT-object size), then we consider the GT
object to be detected, resulting in a TP. If a GT object was not matched/detected by any prediction object we
consider this an FN. If a prediction object could not be matched to a GT object, we consider this an FP. We iterate
over all images and objects in the dataset and obtain all TP, FP, FN for the whole dataset. The final score is then
given by the F1 score (using the determined TPs, FPs, FNs).
Our evaluation code will be available here: https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/mood

b) Justify why the metric(s) was/were chosen, preferably with reference to the biomedical application.





                                  Medical Out-of-Distribution Analysis Challenge 2024

We chose this metric in contrast to AP since this better matched the objective of localizing and detecting an
abnromal image part. AP, similar to dice, tends to put unproportional importance on 'big' objects, which, even
despite batching, can mask some undetected objects. Here an object-detection-based metric can be more fitting.
We opted for this center of mass and size-based matching and not an IoU-based score since we found this better
aligns with the detection of an object which could then be presented to a physician for further review than an
arbitrary IoU threshold. An expert radiologist confirmed this to be a reasonable approach.
tasks.registered_ranking_text:
a) Describe the method used to compute a performance rank for all submitted algorithms based on the generated
metric results on the test cases. Typically the text will describe how results obtained per case and metric are
aggregated to arrive at a final score/ranking.

Since scans in the test set can be normal and contain no anomalies and scans might contain multiple anomalies, a
per-case score is not optimal (as it would have a high per-scan variance and give very extreme values). Thus we
first calculate a whole-dataset score and then combine the different datasets with consolidation ranking (giving
both datasets the same importance). This code has been previously tested on multiple in-house projects (e.g. [26]
) where the predictions have been reviewed by an expert radiologist and the code was made public for last year's
edition.

b) Describe the method(s) used to manage submissions with missing results on test cases.

Since we use docker-based testing we assume that almost all participants will process all cases. However, should
one case be not considered, we will assign it 0 TPs, FPs, and FNs (similar to an 'all 0' prediction).

c) Justify why the described ranking scheme(s) was/were used.

For each voxel, the users should report an anomaly score, indicating the certainty of detecting the anomaly for
the given voxels. We expect the scores to be in the interval [0-1], where 0 is the lowest score indicating no
abnormality and 1 is the highest score indicating the most abnormal input (Scores above and below the interval
will be clamped to [0-1]) or binary [0,1]. We will use the reported scores together with the ground truth labels to
calculate the TPs, FPs, FNs over the whole dataset. The ranking for one dataset will then be given by the F1 over
the whole dataset (given the TPs, FPs, FNs). We combine the two datasets by choosing a consolidation ranking
schema.
